extracted.intended_audience: Illinois voters / Republican supporters / general 1858 electorate
extracted.subtask_description: Rhetorical and argumentative norms illustrated by Abraham Lincoln's 1858 campaign speeches — how to frame political claims, rebut opponents, use constitutional/history arguments, and focus campaign messaging. Useful for composing persuasive political addresses in electoral contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish prediction from advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: When I said ... 'I do not expect the Union to be dissolved,' ... I did not say that I was in favor of anything in it. I only said what I expected would take place. I made a prediction only,--it may have been a foolish one, perhaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear whether a statement is a prediction of likely outcomes or an endorsement of those outcomes; correct misinterpretations promptly to avoid being charged with advocating undesired actions. Lincoln uses this to rebut Douglas's claim that his words favored war or forcible uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid drawing unwarranted inferences from language
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge Douglas ... draws this inference from the language I have quoted to you. He says that I am in favor of making all the States of this Union uniform ... He draws this inference from the language I have quoted to you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not permit opponents to infer broad or extreme positions from careful or predictive wording; explain original meaning and refuse 'quibbles' over words when they distort intent. Provide concrete clarification and restatement if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect principle of self-government; limit federal interference
rubrics_metrics.description: I have said, very many times, ... that no man believed more than I in the principle of self-government; ... each community as a State has a right to do exactly as it pleases with all the concerns within that State that interfere with the right of no other State; and that the General Government, upon principle, has no right to interfere with anything other than that general class of things that does concern the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing about federal versus state power, articulate a clear principle: federal government should act only on matters concerning the whole nation; leave local/domestic regulations (e.g., cranberry, oyster, liquor laws) to states unless they affect other states' rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical and constitutional evidence to ground claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The adoption of the Constitution and its attendant history led the people to believe so; and that such was the belief of the framers of the Constitution itself, why did those old men ... decree that slavery should not go into the new Territory ... Why declare that within twenty years the African slave trade ... might be cut off by Congress?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support political and legal positions by pointing to constitutional text, framers' intent, and historical legislative acts; enumerate concrete historical acts as indicators of original expectations (e.g., prohibitions on slavery in new territories, slave trade limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand judicial decisions' dual role and pursue lawful reversal when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the uses of decisions of courts? They have two uses. As rules of property they have two uses. First, they decide upon the question before the court. ... That is, they say that when a question comes up ... it will be so decided again ... unless the court overrules its decision. Well, we mean to do what we can to have the court decide the other way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize court rulings both as case-specific resolutions and as precedents; if a decision is deemed erroneous or unjust, seek peaceful, legal means (legislation, later court decisions) to reverse or limit its effect rather than treating it as sacrosanct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uphold the Declaration's equality principle as a normative standard
rubrics_metrics.description: When they look through that old Declaration of Independence, they find that those old men say that 'We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal'; and then they feel that that moral sentiment ... evidences their relation to those men ... That is the electric cord in that Declaration ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Declaration of Independence as a moral and rhetorical touchstone to unify diverse audiences and to justify claims for equal rights; treat it as an aspirational standard to approximate even if full attainment is not yet possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject racial-inferiority arguments and their political analogues
rubrics_metrics.description: Those arguments that are made, that the inferior race are to be treated with as much allowance as they are capable of enjoying; ... They are the arguments that kings have made for enslaving the people in all ages of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter arguments that justify subjugation on alleged inferiority by pointing out their historical use to legitimize oppression; equate such reasoning with discredited doctrines (e.g., kingcraft) to expose moral and political danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus campaign messaging on substantive issues, not trappings
rubrics_metrics.description: Auxiliary to these main points, to be sure, are their thunderings of cannon, their marching and music, their fizzlegigs and fireworks; but I will not waste time with them. They are but the little trappings of the campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clear exposition of core issues (e.g., popular sovereignty, Dred Scott) over spectacle; use rhetoric to illuminate substance rather than distract with pageantry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain party principles over personal loyalty to leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: If you indorse him, you tell him you do not care whether slavery be voted up or down ... That is the question. If Republican men have been in earnest in what they have done, I think they had better not do it; but I think that the Republican party is made up of those who ... will oppose the extension of slavery, and who will hope for its ultimate extinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage voters and party members to hold leaders accountable to party principles; do not let personal popularity or promise of patronage override fundamental commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer substantive critique over petty quibbling
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge Douglas informed you that this speech of mine was probably carefully prepared. I admit that it was. I am not master of language; ... But I don't care about a quibble in regard to words. I know what I meant, and I will not leave this crowd in doubt, if I can explain it to them, what I really meant in the use of that paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When engaging in debate, avoid getting bogged down in hair-splitting semantic disputes; explain intent plainly and return to substantive matters of principle and policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address popular misconceptions by explicit explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: He says I am in favor of making war by the North upon the South for the extinction of slavery ... Now, it is singular enough ... that I did not say that I was in favor of anything in it. I only said what I expected would take place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and correct common misunderstandings of your positions via clear, explicit restatement; use public addresses to dispel false charges and to restate the practical implications of your views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public commemorations to connect history with present civic identity
rubrics_metrics.description: These 4th of July gatherings I suppose have their uses. ... We hold this annual celebration to remind ourselves of all the good done in this process of time ... and we go from these meetings in better humor with ourselves, we feel more attached the one to the other, and more firmly bound to the country we inhabit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage anniversaries and public ceremonies to remind citizens of founding principles, to unify diverse populations, and to strengthen commitment to national ideals.
